utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated and have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning to the Defence counsel, to the Prosecution. We will work for a little while now. Let's have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the ELMO, Mr. President, could be placed by the witness, I think that needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume our work. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, as you know, this morning there was another case before the Trial Chamber and it took a bit longer than we thought it would. We can now resume. Mr. Hayman, the floor is yours, you can work until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Good morning and good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Whatley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me touch on two subjects before continuing with the April 8th events of 1993 that we were discussing. First, you mentioned that you had meetings with commanders of both warring parties six or seven days a week during your tour. At what level or levels of command or units were these regular contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My most usual level of command that I had contact with was at the brigade level. It wasn't exclusively a brigade level, I also dealt with the higher levels, which in the case of the HVO was Colonel Blaskic, and in the case of the Bosnian army was General Hadzihasanovic in Zenica, and on occasions with lower level commanders, below the level of brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned yesterday your introduction, if you will, to the region on your drive north on the road from Gornji Vakuf to Novi Travnik in the middle or latter part of October, 1992. When you first arrived in Vitez during that same time period, what did you find with respect to the relationship between the HVO and the BH army in Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On about, I suppose it must have been about the 20th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, October, 1992. The Bosnian army and the HVO in Vitez were undergoing a small war. There was shooting in the town. There was HVO soldiers in front of Hotel Vitez when shooting at Bosnian army positions, and fire was being returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to return to the 8th of April, 1993, where we left our work yesterday. You had described a meeting with commanders of both sides in the city of Travnik on that day, and specifically you described the fact that you had been told, among other things, that the HVO headquarters in Travnik had moved out of the town to a location known as Dolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If a new map, Mr. President, which we have marked during the recess as Defence Exhibit 418, if that could perhaps be folded by the witness so that the portion of the map indicating Travnik and adjacent areas could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Complies)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, the city of Travnik, it is marked, but for convenience, if you could indicate Travnik on the map, Defence Exhibit 418?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the town of Travnik here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Travnik an urban area for the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's the main centre of population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the area or areas of Dolac, where you were told, on the 8th of April, the HVO had moved its headquarters out of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dolac is to the east of Travnik, this area here. I must point out this is a very old map, and the town is quite more built up than it appears here, but Dolac is this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating to the east, south-east of the city of Travnik itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can put that map aside for now. I direct your attention to two days later, the 10th of April, 1993. Did you learn on the 10th of further incidents between the BH army and the HVO that had occurred the night before, on the 9th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a meeting on the Saturday morning, the 10th of April, 1993. I had a meeting with Baba Salko in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Baba Salko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Baba Salko was one of my main Bosnian army contacts who dealt with -- he ran the exchange commission in Travnik, which was concerned with exchanging prisoners of war, dead bodies, and moving refugees across the front-lines with the Serbs. His additional duties were to act. He was one of the people who liaised with me from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from him of any incidents in the town of Travnik on the prior day of the 9th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me there was a bomb in the hotel. He is referring there to Hotel Orient, which was an HVO accommodation hotel, and at a church. He told me there was a bomb directed against 7 Brigade, which was the 7th Muslim Brigade. He told me at 2355 hours, the night before there had been shooting in the town for about half an hour, and that a cafe had been destroyed in Dolac, and that a hand grenade had been thrown in the Bosnian army barracks, and that later on, that at half past midnight the previous evening, an 82 millimetre recoilless weapon had been fired in the town as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the level of tension or conflict, then, as of the night of the 9th of April, 1993, in Travnik, based on those reports which you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The level of tension in Travnik at this stage was very, very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the 12th of April, 1993, two days later. Did you visit Travnik again on the 12th of April? Could you tell us what you learned on that visit with respect to the situation in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Monday, the 12th of April, 1993, I visited the Bosnian army in Travnik and spoke to the deputy commander there. He listed many of the things which had gone on in the town the previous evening, including a large explosion that started, well, an explosion that happened at 10.30 or sometime between 10.30 and 11.00, and a series of explosions, with the strongest one at 0300 hours on the morning of the 12th. He also confirmed that on the Saturday night, referring to the previous part of this, that there had been an RPG fired south of the road. It's not clear which road he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also meet on the 12th of April, 1993 with Colonel Filipovic, the HVO commander in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was, I think, probably the next meeting of the day. I went to see Colonel Filipovic, and among other things he told me that the 7th Muslim Brigade were causing the problems, that the police in the town were useless, that they had no will, and the politicians in the town would not talk to each other because of the flag burning incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have another meeting with the HVO in their Dolac headquarters later in the day on the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at 1410 hours I went to Dolac to the HVO headquarters there, and I spoke to Commander Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have heard in this trial of Franjo Nakic. Are you referring to Franjo Nakic or some other Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it is Franjo Nakic, but I don't know the first name of this chap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this person a local HVO commander in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he was not somebody with whom I was very familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from him of any incidents that were ongoing or had recently occurred in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he listed -- I got five points that he made here, but probably the most important one: He stated that the HVO had been killed in their flats by the Mecici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the Mecici were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mecici in Travnik, and we were becoming aware of this. The Mecici in Travnik was a criminal group, a very well armed criminal group that was terrorising the Croat population in Travnik at the beginning of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Mecici a powerful force in Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the Bosnian army commanders in Travnik and the HVO referred to them frequently, and said they were too powerful for the police to deal with because they were armed with rifles. They were from the town and knew the town very well. This is what we believed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned checkpoints. Did you attribute any significance during your tour of duty to the appearance or removal of checkpoints in the region and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We always considered checkpoints as a barometer of the level of tension in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain? You mean barometer in both directions, up and down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if tension was rising or had risen as a result of killings or house burnings or political statements on the television or whatever, then very quickly checkpoints would appear all over the place. They were used by the local communities as a way of defending their community from outsiders, because this was a very mixed Croat Muslim area. So, a Croat village, they would erect a checkpoint on its part of the road or maybe two, and the Muslims would and the Croats would, and all of a sudden you would have 20 or 30 checkpoints in the space of an hour or two arriving. Then as the tension went down, the number of checkpoints would reduce back to the, what we considered to be the standard level of checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, you just passed very quickly on the Mecici. Were they Serbs or Muslims? Could you just let us know what it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. I apologise if I'm going too quickly or rushing the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain, Mr. Whatley, the Mecici; what was the composition of that criminal group, to the extent you received information about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Mecici were a criminal group based in Travnik, and I believe, although I have no first-hand knowledge, I believe they were majority Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you mean by majority? Were there other Muslims or Croats or Serbs, or was it just a terrorist group, nothing to do with the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to describe them as a terrorist group, but they may have been that. They were described to me as, if you like, an independent criminal group that was very well armed from the town, and it was terrorising the Croat population. That's what I was told. I can assume they were probably not Croats and Serbs, because there were very few Serbs left in Travnik at the time we're talking about. You could almost assume they were probably all Muslim; but I was never told that, so I would be very careful as to say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about this group, the Mecici, only on the one occasion you identified, or did you hear about them many times from the parties to the conflict in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name Mecici did come up many times, but I can't remember how many times. We were well aware by this time, now, the middle of April, 1993, that they existed. They were a criminal gang, and looking back, they had an enormous effect on what was going on in Travnik. We were probably not aware of that until too late. We were still more preoccupied with the military commanders rather than the criminal gangs and their relationship to the law and order and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the 12th of April, 1993, you've describe two meetings with HVO commanders. Did you also meet with representatives of the BH army at their headquarters in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything from them concerning the situation in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at 1830 hours on the evening of the 12th of April I had a meeting with the Bosnian army in Travnik, and amongst other things, and I will read exactly what my notebook says, it's point five: "About 4.00 p.m. Dolac checkpoint not moved, no power, Bruno, Knights, Mostar."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a quote from your contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a quote. On the next page there are more notes on the same meeting referring to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to the other notations, let me ask you, you said three words that may need to be, well, four, that may need to be dissected a bit. Dolac, is that the location where the HVO headquarters had moved to out of Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the BH commander was telling you that the checkpoint at Dolac had not moved, what would you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, the military commanders, Colonel Filipovic and Colonel Alagic, in Travnik, of the HVO and Bosnian army, were constantly trying to reduce the tension and also reduce the number of checkpoints which were interfering with the civilian population. What this refers to, I believe, is that the Bosnian army were telling me that the HVO in Travnik did not have the power to remove this checkpoint because it was not under their command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the last three words of the passage you have quoted for the Court. "Bruno Knights, Mostar," when you use the word "Knights," is the word in your notes, is it "nights" as in day and night, or is it "Knights" as in Knights of the round table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the word "Knights" spelled with a K.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were you aware at the time that there was a group in Vitez known as the Vitez Knights or Vitezovi and used the term Knights with a K as their name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that the Minister of Defence of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar was Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn later on the 12th, or in that same conversation, of a later in time checkpoint or checkpoint problem from the BH command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this meeting started at 1830, and one of the points that came up in the meeting was that at 1700 hours, at 5.00 p.m. that day, and I quote "Knights commander who put the checkpoint at the BH headquarters." It doesn't say outside, but I've I said outside, then it says "312 command." If I could explain that? I questioned him in this meeting about some details about what he was talking about with this checkpoint, because I didn't understand. He said that at 5.00 p.m. the Knights, which I then began to realise was a unit of the Croat unit, it was the commander who put the checkpoint outside the Bosnian headquarters of 312 Brigade in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been a provocative act to put a Croat checkpoint outside of a BH army Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very provocative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a BH army brigade in the Travnik area known as the 312th Brigade of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were three brigades in Travnik and one of them was 312 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a document I would like to show the witness, Mr. President, if the usher could assist. It consists of one page, it is an annexe to a Cheshire Regiment MILINFOSUM that was provided to the Defence by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D419.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If there's an extra copy, perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could read this document, please, and tell us if you recognise the subject matter referred to in the document. Do you recognise the subject matter of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dated, in that it's an annexe to a MILINFOSUM which was dated the 13th of April, 1993. At or about this time, or on the prior day, the 12th of April, 1993, was a joint commission of one sort or another formed in Travnik between the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document memorialise the conclusions of that joint commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a translation of the conclusions of the formation of the commission, a translation done by the British interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, and I will read it, states: "Joint commissions are to ensure that all the agreed points are implemented. If they are not, the commission is to intervene. Captain M. Dundas-Whatley will join the commission as an UNPROFOR representative. The joint commission's aim is to make sure all trenches are filled in." Is that a reference to yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, subsequent to this event, participate for some period of time in the work of this joint commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose with respect to filling in trenches? What was the purpose of the commission's work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the major indications of problems in Travnik, and indeed one of the main problems in Travnik, was that on the high ground around the town, both the Bosnian army and the HVO had been placing machine gun positions, heavy machine gun positions, and on occasions these machine guns would then fire into different parts of the town. The Croat ones firing into Muslim areas and vice versa. The purpose of the commission was to get the guns off the hills, back into the barracks, fill in the trenches, reduce the tension so that the HVO and the Bosnian army could continue the war against what they called the common enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The common enemy being --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This translation indicates that the signatories to this document were Colonel Filipovic and Alagic. Were they the brigade commanders of the HVO and BH army units in Travnik, respectively, or did they have some other positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the commanders of the HVO and the BiH, respectively, in Travnik, but certainly in the case of Colonel Alagic, he was a much more senior level than brigade commander. He had under his command more than three brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By this document, how would you characterise what these two commanders were trying to do at this critical juncture, the 12th or 13th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were doing what many, in many areas of Bosnia, the HVO and Bosnian army were trying to do, was to stop a war starting between the HVO and the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 of the conclusions of the joint commission states: "HVO, BiH commanders and civil police commanders have agreed that they are to establish full control over their soldiers in the aim of peacekeeping in the area." Were you receiving information at or about this time that on both sides of the conflict there were units of soldiers, or other armed persons, who were outside the control of the military structures on the HVO and/or BiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were. I was constantly being approached by the military commanders on both sides during the meetings, and them complaining to me, or using me as someone to explain the problems they were having controlling criminal organisations in the area. By criminal organisations, I mean highly armed quasi military criminal gangs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can put this document aside for the moment. Thank you. Let me direct your attention to the next day, the 13th of April, 1993. On the 13th of April did you learn of the kidnapping of certain HVO officers from or in the region of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whom you met with and what you learned concerning the kidnapping of these three officers and a driver, or four officers, as the case may be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon of the 13th of April, 1993, I went to Novi Travnik. Would you like me to indicate that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can probably do it sitting down so you can hear me. This is the town of Travnik, and this is the town of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate Vitez so we have a reference point, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the town of Novi Travnik probably in the afternoon, although I have haven't written the time of the meeting, and I spoke to the HVO commander in Novi Travnik. His name was Zeljko Sabljic. He told me that, "Three people plus the driver, Bugojno Road, 1400 hours, sentry ports, car."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling us what the notations in your notebook are on this matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it exactly. If I can explain what that means? He was telling me that three members of the HVO plus their driver, who were travelling on the Bugojno Road -- perhaps you want me to point that road out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps, if you can, if that has a clear and determinant meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll point out the road of Novi Travnik and then which road is the Bugojno Road from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating to south/south-west from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a very well-made road but it heads to the town of Bugojno. At 1400 hours this incident had happened from their car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO commander know where these four abductees were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my notes, he believed that it was perpetrated by the 7th Muslim Brigade but there's a question mark there. He went on to say that he had already phoned Mevludin, and Mevludin was the Bosnia army commander in the town of Novi Travnik. He'd already phoned him to ask him to phone the 7th Muslim Brigade, and that had already been done. He then told me that the people in the incident that had disappeared, two members were HVO soldiers, and then the two others, one was the deputy commander of the 1st battalion of an HVO brigade, but I don't know -- presumably his brigade but it doesn't say that here, and it gives me the name of that deputy commander as Ivica Kamdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you characterise the effect of this apparent kidnapping, on the 13th of April, 1993, on the level of tension in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Novi Travnik this had a major effect. Checkpoints sprung up everywhere and the tension level went very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, on the 13th of April, 1993, did you meet with Sefkija Djidic in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Sefkija Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefkija Djidic was the Bosnian army officer in the old part of Vitez known as Stari Vitez. He was not a brigade commander. He was a lower level commander. We used to call him the town commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from Mr. Djidic, on the 13th of April, 1993, of another incident that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that -- and it's probably best I just read it from the notebook and explain it afterwards. He told me, "Forest, opened fire, damaged vehicle, Darko Kraljevic, commander HOS." What he was telling me about there is an attempt at murdering Mr. Darko Kraljevic by people opening fire from woodland. They damaged the vehicle but they did not kill Mr. Darko Kraljevic, whom Sefkija Djidic believed was the commander of the HOS, a Croat -- an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to leave the 13th of April, 1993 and move forward to the 15th of April, 1993. First, on the morning of the 15th of April, did you have a meeting with the HVO command in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, at 0935 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you learn from them concerning further incidents in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke to the HVO deputy commander, who, amongst other things, told me that the 7th Muslim Brigade had put a checkpoint outside the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reference to the hotel would be what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO -- sorry, the hotel that he's referring to was the headquarters of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was his headquarters, the HVO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a celebration on the part of the BH army on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of April, 1993 was the first anniversary of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any celebrations of this event on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Following these meetings in Novi Travnik, I went to Travnik. I'd been invited to do this a few days before. I went to the main Bosnian army headquarters in Travnik where I was a guest of Colonel Filipovic at the celebration parade for the first anniversary of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Colonel Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Alagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Colonel Filipovic present at the parade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, we have a small photograph that I'd like to place on the ELMO and question the witness about. I would ask that if it's possible, that a copy be made so the witness can retain a copy at the end of the trial or what have you. If we could mark it and put it on the ELMO, please, as the next exhibit in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you agree that we will keep the original then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I agree. I think the witness has a sentimental attachment to the photograph. He's in the photograph, but if a professional copy could be made of the photograph, I think that that will meet the witness's needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me turn to the witness. Mr. Whatley, it's your photograph, it's your document, and I understand you appear in that picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, it would appear normal that the photograph be given back to you if a visible copy can be made so that it could be tendered into evidence. That way you could go home with your photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This photograph is D420, and the document that the registrar will have will be a copy of the one which is being shown now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could go just very slightly left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle of the picture, this is me here in uniform, and on the left here is my interpreter. This photograph was taken in Travnik on the morning of the 15th of April, 1993, and, in fact, you can see the date written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 15th of April, 1993. These were -- many of the senior Bosnian army and Bosnian government figures in Travnik on the morning of that parade. We're all standing on what in Britain we would call a saluting dais. Taking the salute at the front here, the senior officer present is Colonel Alagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indicating at the far right-hand side or end of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Colonel Alagic, who was the senior Bosnian army commander for Travnik. Over here with -- appears to be smoking, with his hand in front of his mouth, is Commander Kulenovic, who was one of our main contacts as well, and he was the town commander for Travnik for the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's the individual second from the left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. In uniform between the two civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the festivities? Was there a parade, and if so, was it a large parade or how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was very large parade that morning, the largest collection of locals in uniform that we had seen in one place. Certainly in excess of a thousand soldiers, but I don't know how many. I think the parade probably went on for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the ceremony, did you receive word that you were needed elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was asked to go to Zenica. My Land Rover, which is parked slightly to right of this picture, off and behind, you can't see it. My radio operator came to me and told me he'd received a message telling me that I should proceed immediately to the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to extract yourself from the ceremony or did that make you uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was slightly awkward, but I saluted Colonel Alagic and I then left the parade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit D416, which is a map we marked yesterday, could be provided to the witness and put on the ELMO it would be helpful. It is one of the JNA map series, Zenica 4, D416. We can proceed with exhibit -- if we have it, that would be fine. If we could provide it to the witness, and perhaps the witness can fold the map so that the road from Vitez to Zenica, the so-called mountain road, will be visible on the ELMO. Could you indicate for the Court on what route you proceeded to Zenica on the -- what was by now what, the late morning or midday of the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the time was probably about midday. Could you just pull -- I'm sorry to try and control what's going on in the court here, but -- that's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate how you travelled to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This road here goes to Travnik, up this way to -- and I drove down this road from Travnik, past the British base, which was about here, along this main road here, which is not marked because the map's too old, and up this mountain road here to Zenica. Zenica is here. I carried on up the mountain road here, and then we started to go down here, and this is the village of Cajdras here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find when you reached Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Cajdras I encountered a reinforced HVO checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you proceed on to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO checkpoint had put mines in the road, which was a severe indication of the tension level, but I told my driver just to ignore the mines and to drive straight into Zenica, and we did not stop at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find in Zenica at midday on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica is a large city and I went there frequently, but on this day it was completely different to how it normally looked. Normally the city would be bustling with shoppers. On this occasion the streets were deserted. There were military policemen and soldiers, armed soldiers, standing on the corners of the streets, and there were a couple of buses blocking some -- a couple of the streets as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you proceed and did you meet, during your visit to Zenica, with the representative of the HVO at the HVO headquarters in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name or first name of that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to what I believed to be the deputy commander of the HVO in Zenica, whose name I wrote down as Vinko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you learned by this time that the HVO brigade commander had been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that there had been a kidnapping in the city but I didn't know the details at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the scene of the kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went with -- excuse me. I went with commander Vinko to the scene in my Land Rover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In very short summary, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found a car, a silver Audi 80, the number plate I have here, which had been abandoned. It was full of bullet holes and full of blood. There were no people left in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At or about that time, or after perhaps returning to the HVO headquarters, did you have a conversation with Vinko, the deputy commander, and if so, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He, having shown me the results of this incident, and it was rather horrific, then I went back to his office in the hotel and he briefed me, and if I could read directly from my notebook. Point one, "More killed by Muslims than Chetniks." What he's referring to there is he believes that more Croats were being killed by the Muslims than by the Serbs. Point two, "Who is enemy?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that did you understand him to mean who is the enemy of the Croats in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, who is his enemy. He felt that he was fighting against the Serbs, the people referred to as Chetniks, but on his own doorstep his commander is kidnapped by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give any more information concerning the kidnapping to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said, three, "Corps did nothing." That is a reference to the corps headquarters of the Bosnian army based in Zenica. Fourth point, "7th Muslim Brigade not wanted here by other brigades." This was a repeated complaint by both the Bosnian army and the HVO, that the presence of the 7th Muslim Brigade was not wanted by the HVO or the normal Bosnian army brigades in the various towns. He then said that there were 1.300 extremists in 7th Muslim brigade, and then he told me about an ultimatum he received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he received that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The ultimatum came in by telephone that day. He said if -- I quote, "If they don't release Mujahedeen in Busovaca in 48 hours, we'll kill Zivko Totic." It then says, "Commander, 2nd Brigade, HVO." Would you like me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near Busovaca, which I -- would you like to point Busovaca out on the map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll point Zenica first. On this one, not the other one. That's Zenica, the big city where I was at the time, and this is the town of Busovaca. In or near the town of Busovaca, we knew that the HVO had a prison, and we knew that in the prison were many foreign people from the Middle East who had been arrested. I think we were aware of 12 by name at this stage, maybe more. This ultimatum is saying, "You let the Arabs go and you can have your commander Totic back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was a little more explicit than that, that if they weren't released in 48 hours Totic would be killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with the 15th of April, 1993, later on that day did you visit the BH army commands in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn of a new incident on the 15th of April, 1993 from the BH army representative you met with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At 1955 hours that evening in Vitez, at the Bosnian army headquarters in the town, I was told that three members of the Bosnian army had been arrested by the HVO in Vitez, and that it had happened at 0515, and that they were members of the Bosnian army Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn any more about that incident an hour or so later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At 2100 hours that evening, I went back to speak to commander Sefkija, and he gave me a little bit more detail. He said that it had happened at 1715, and that he gave me the names of the two Bosnian army military policemen who had been kidnapped, and their names were Spahic Fahrudin and Hurem Semko. He gave me a third name in addition, but subsequently the third person was recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that that third person had already been recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure. Sometime afterwards, I had crossed it out and put a tick next to it to say that it was no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sefkija Djidic tell you, on the evening of the 15th, where he believed two of the three missing BH army military policemen had been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, and I'll read it. He said, "Taken from house by HVO to elementary school, Dubravica, (HVO)."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that the Dubravica school, near Vitez, was the headquarters of the Vitezovi or Vitez Knights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was aware that the school in Dubravica was an HVO location, but I did not know which unit was based there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn, in this meeting with Sefkija Djidic, any other provocations, from his perspective, that had occurred on the night of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said at 2130 hours that a few soldiers had been disarmed near Stari Bila, which was -- I think probably best point that out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could zoom in, and perhaps you can move the map to the left. If we could zoom in on Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 416, and could you point out Stari Bila, where you were told some BH army soldiers had been disarmed on the evening of the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I received the information here in Vitez, talking to commander Sefkija, but the place he was referring to was one and a half kilometres away here in Stari Bila, which was also the British base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stari Bila is indicated in blue on Exhibit D416; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been highlighted in blue here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what you recall or what your notes reflect concerning this incident of the disarming of some number of BH army soldiers near Stari Bila? When was it and who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, and I recall very little, but I can read to you from my notebook. It says, "2130 hours, few soldiers disarmed near Stari Bila. Darko Kraljevic, guy shot at. Bruno Stojic, Mostar Knights."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was something that was told to you by Sefkija Djidic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand the connection to be during this incident, the disarming of soldiers, and Darko Kraljevic, the guy shot at. What was the connection, as you understand your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Darko Kraljevic, somebody who I didn't know but whose name appears in my notebook, he is the Croat who had been, the day before, two days before, or maybe even three days before, there had been an attempt on his life in the town or near Vitez somewhere, and that's what "guy shot at" means. It's a reference in my notebook, so I knew we were talking about the same guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the level of tension at this point on the evening of the 15th? You were learning of these cumulative incidents. How would you characterise the level of tension in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evening of the 15th of April, 1993 was when the level of tension had reached its highest level in the time that -- in the six months, at that stage, that I had been in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that evening, the night of the 15th of April, 1993, do you recall whether any BH army commanders made any threats to you concerning possible BH army attacks on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There's a certain amount of confusion in my mind as to exactly where this threat was given to me, whether it was by Sefkija in Stari Vitez or by the commander in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "the commander in Kruscica" you mean the BH commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian army had a headquarters in Kruscica and elsewhere, of course. Yes, I do remember a threat being given to me, and the threat was, "If the two Bosnian army military policemen that had been kidnapped are not released, I, as the commander, cannot be responsible for the actions of my soldiers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the British battalion's assessment at the time that this meant that imminent retaliation by the BH army was likely, that is against -- by the BH army against the HVO was likely unless the two missing BH army personnel were recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my assessment and the assessment of the MILINFO officer as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was on the night of the 15th of April, 1993 that that threat or threats were made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the night of the 15th of April, 1993, did you report to the command of the British battalion that Vitez was in imminent danger of exploding into conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I reported it to the second in command, Major Brian Watters, and I reported it to the MILINFOSUM, and I think also to the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a recommendation concerning how the British battalion might attempt to calm the situation in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I wanted to continue -- two things. I wanted to, firstly, continue my efforts to track down and have those two policemen released to an avoid further conflict. That was my first recommendation. Secondly, I suggested that the British send Warrior armoured fighting vehicles into the town, because that had been very successful in the past at helping to diffuse tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were those recommendations followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. Certainly, I was told not to continue my efforts personally, because it was considered too dangerous for me to be in the town, and secondly, I believe no Warriors were sent into the town that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've previously mentioned a lot of incidents in Travnik, and here on the 15th of April, 1993, we're speaking more of Vitez. Had the focus, in your eyes and in the eyes of the British Battalion, of the danger of eminent conflict, had it shifted by the night of the 15th of April from Travnik to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, your six or seven months in Central Bosnia, did anyone on either the BH army or the HVO side express any concern or even interest to you concerning any ultimatum issued by the HVO in Herzegovina concerning the formation of a joint command between the BH army and the HVO on or before the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone, either on the BH army or the HVO side, express any interest or even knowledge of such an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was. The whole issue was to do with the Vance-Owen Plan, which was a peace plan put forward by Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen. As a result of that plan, parts of Bosnia were to be controlled by different entities. The region we're talking about now was to become, I think it was going to be called Canton 10, I can't remember, and it was going to be a Croat canton. So the Croat authorities in Mostar considered that they should take control of this area, which included the town of Travnik. But, of course, Travnik was overwhelmingly Muslim, particularly in light of the tens of thousands of Muslim refugees from the Serb side, and the Muslims in Travnik were not about to become subordinate to the Croats. I do remember there was a conflict about this. I don't mean shooting, but there was constant talking about this, and various commanders saying "I will never become subordinate to that side" or one side saying "actually we should be in control of this." There was -- yes, there was, but I don't actually remember an ultimatum about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anyone express any knowledge of any specific demand or ultimatum that had to do with a joint command or that had to do with the 15th of April, 1993, specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other than the ultimatum I've just given to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than what you just described in general terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't think of anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next morning, the 16th of April, 1993, of course there was fighting in the region. To your knowledge, was any element of the British Battalion on patrol on the early morning of the 16th of April, 1993, at the time this fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, but I was not involved in the operational side, operation deployment of the Warriors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, then, to the 16th of April, 1993. On the 16th of April, did you meet with an HVO representative in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did at 1845 hours on the evening of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given an appraisal of the situation at that time by the HVO representative you met with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. What the HVO officer said was, "Muslims continuing their attack, new forces from Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we could put up another exhibit, Mr. President, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 45, and I think we will need to put it on the ELMO. It's an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being done, on the 17th of April, 1993, could you tell the Court whether you were asked to escort two HVO negotiators back from a cease-fire meeting, in which the United Nations was involved, back to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think we should wait for the map so you can illustrate these events with the aid of a map. If you could take a moment to orient yourself on this aerial photograph. I believe there is a legend in the upper left-hand corner, if that's of assistance. Have you oriented yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, perhaps it would be helpful if you point out the Hotel Vitez on Prosecutor's Exhibit 45.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Hotel Vitez, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marked as A on this exhibit? Hotel Vitez is marked as A on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can mention the letters if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be helpful. First of all, how did you transport these two negotiators, HVO negotiators, back to the Hotel Vitez on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two negotiators were put into the back of a Warrior, a British armoured fighting vehicle, at our headquarters, which is not on this photograph, over here. I got into the back with them, and with my interpreter. We drove the direct route to the, I think, I seem to remember driving the direct route through the old part of Vitez, here, up the main road, here. We're actually heading south-east, though it is upwards on this photograph. We stopped about here. Now, what you probably are not aware of is actually where I'm pointing to at the moment is a fuel station. At this time the fuel station wasn't functioning, but it is right in front of the hotel, here. The fuel station area and the hotel were completely surrounded in barbed wire in a defensive style.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Why was an armoured vehicle used to transport these two negotiators back to the Hotel Vitez on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a major war going on in Vitez at the time, a lot of shooting, a lot of fighting was happening in Vitez at the time, and it was considered too dangerous for us to travel around, for me to travel around in my Land Rover, which is how I normally travelled, and because we considered it our duty to take every precaution to protect the lives of the HVO negotiators. So we put them into an armoured fighting vehicle, a Warrior, which was the most secure mode of transport available to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far were you able to go in the Warrior towards the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stopped here, by the fuel station. We were probably, I should say about 50 yards from the, maybe slightly less, from the entrance of Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told the driver of the vehicle to open the back door. It was an electrically controlled back door, and then I climbed out of the vehicle with my interpreter, and then the two HVO officers climbed out with me. The back door closed. The vehicle stayed where it was, and I walked with the HVO officers to the front door of Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 45, how you walked? In other words, where were you and in what direction or directions were you walking, the four of you, as you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would like me to point it out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you point it out, and the direction in which were you walking, if it can be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you will be able to see better here. This is the fuel station, and this is the front door of the hotel, here. The Warrior stopped about here, where in fact there's a vehicle already on this photograph. We stopped there, and we walked this way, south -- not south, down on the photograph, along to the right, here, following the line of the barbed wire, and up here, along this long straight, probably 20 yards straight here to the entrance of the hotel, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you and your interpreter and the two HVO negotiators walking? Who was next to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, if you can imagine, I'm on the right, here, I have an HVO officer immediately to my left, another HVO officer to his left, and my interpreter, a girl, to the left of that. We were walking, what we would call four abreast, 1, 2, 3, 4, in a straight line, walking this way towards the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on purpose, to, if you will, sandwich the two negotiators in between the two UNPROFOR personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I was concerned to stay as close to the HVO officers as I could, but it was just the most natural way to walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point here, we were now moving upwards, if you like, at this point here, two yards before we turned to go into the door of the hotel, two shots rang out from behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both HVO officers were hit. One was hit in the hand and the other one was hit in the backside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell the direction from which these two shots were fired and if so, can you indicate on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the photograph here, the shot came from directly behind us, the two shots, in very quick succession, came from directly behind us in this direction down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point with the chopstick you're holding, the direction, perhaps with your hand at the origin of the fire and the end of the chopstick in the direction that these two rounds headed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I point like that, where my fingers, my fingers indicate where we were, and the stick is pointing to the direction that the rounds came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that at the lower end of the chopstick, where you're indicating below the Hotel Vitez? What area is that and under whose control was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't entirely certain as to which buildings had been captured by which side, but subsequently, I learned this area was controlled by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that area, was there a field of vision to the location where the two negotiators were shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell whether two shots were fired from the same weapon or two different weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say for certain, but the impression I had at the time was it was probably two separate weapons, because of the very quick succession between the rounds. Of course it could have been fired from one weapon, an automatic, but I think it is unlikely, but I can never be certain, because of the accuracy with which they fired. The person firing or the people firing took a great risk at that range not to hit me, as a member of the United Nations, or my interpreter, who was also dressed as United Nations, she had a blue barrier on as well. We were so close, I believe it was probably two separate snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From a sniper rifle is it possible to fire two shots in as close a succession as these two shots were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe that most sniper rifles have to be loaded, each round has to be loaded separately. Of course, there could be automatically loading sniper rifles that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This would be a convenient breaking point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, this will be the time for the break, I suggest we resume at 3.00 and we will meet from 3.00 to 6.00. We will resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then have the witness brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I would like to move now to the 18th of April, 1993. On or after that date did you have occasion to visit the site of a large explosion in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how long after the explosion it was that you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the date, but I would say it was probably about a week or so after the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasion of your visit to the scene, did you witness the recovery of any bodies from the wreckage of a building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the international press present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was the largest collection of international media and television cameras that I ever saw in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The very large truck bomb which had exploded in Stari Vitez had destroyed or taken the roofs off something in the order of 40 houses, and many of the houses were very badly damaged. The object of this particular day was for us to provide -- us as UNPROFOR, to provide security, in other words, using our Warriors to protect the local workers in the town who were going to work on one house which they believed had people trapped inside it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a recovery operation undertaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The British Royal Engineers assisted the local soldiers to slowly, piece by piece, remove the stones from the collapsed building so they could get to the people inside that had been crushed when the building fell over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. We had been told there were some civilians caught inside the building. The reality, of course, when we dismantled the building and got to the bodies inside, there were actually three armed and uniformed soldiers who had been killed in the explosion, and as the house collapsed, were crushed under the rubble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when these bodies were found and recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The locals who were doing most of the work were very anxious that the media that were filming all this, and all the media were on one side of the house, behind some white tape which we had erected. They were anxious that the media did not see the weapons coming out of the house. So as the bodies were lifted out of the house, the weapons were hidden in coats and carried off to the back, out of view of the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of weapons they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were just the standard issue Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attribute any significance to the concealment of these weapons from the press present at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was perfectly normal. I didn't speak to the press about this. We considered ourselves to be beyond telling the press this type of, if you like, secret, but it was perfectly normal. All sides probably, but certainly both sides, were very skilful in their manipulation of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance in handing out a document, please. The document, Mr. President, consists of two pages. It is in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D421.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you get this document, if you could look at it and tell us whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a translation of a document produced in Travnik by Colonel Filipovic and Colonel Alagic, relating to a meeting which had taken place, an agreement which had been reached between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you obtain this document on or about the 19th of April, 1993, which is the date in the first line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Probably the 19th, but it may have been -- this translation may have been given to me the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who made the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was made in the interpreter's office of the British base, so it would have been one of our -- judging by the writing, I think probably one of our local interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide this document to me prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to locate a copy of the B/S/C original of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That would be held in the British archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I won't read the whole document, but I'd like to read, perhaps, the introduction and the first paragraph or two. It is titled "Notice," and begins, "On the day of 19 April, 1993, a meeting was held in Travnik between the commands of the HVO and the BiH army regarding the practical realisation of the documents signed and agreed on by Mr. A. Izetbegovic and Mr. M. Boban on 18 April, 1993. Following the order of this document and facing the danger of the common enemy, the two commands have decided to inform the complete Travnik public about the following: One, the HVO and BiH army commands will undertake all measures and means at their disposal, and those include force, to protect Croat and Muslim people against any possible clashes and attacks by extreme forces and orientations. Two, in this context, all forces erecting non-negotiated or self-decided barricades or checkpoints, and those mistreating the population will be prevented from doing that. The initiators and realisers of such activities will be forced to go to the front-line against the common enemy. This also stands for those who prowl the town with rifles without executing their professional duty. This matter will be regulated by a separate order." I'll read one more paragraph: "Three, the two commands resolutely demand that the civil government immediately put its authority and functions into the service of peacekeeping and protection of all population, public order and peace, and that they do not contribute in any way towards negative development of this situation." It continues, Mr. President, in paragraph four to talk about public information and the regulation of unconfirmed information being released to the public. The remaining paragraphs discuss other matters along this same vein. My question is: In your view, did this joint statement or notice by Commander Filipovic and Commander Alagic, did it reflect the sincere desires of both commanders of the HVO and BH army in Travnik to implement and support the agreement of 18 April, 1993 between Messrs. Izetbegovic and Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your first-hand involvement and knowledge of the conflict in Central Bosnia from October 1992 until May of 1993, can you tell the Court, in your opinion, what was the degree of command and control that existed within the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult for us to make an assessment of the command and control that Colonel Blaskic exercised over the HVO in middle Bosnia. We did not have the detailed information about the workings of the HVO headquarters in Vitez, but we did learn of many incidents from which it appeared that the chain of command was flimsy, and overall we felt that -- well, I feel now, and I probably felt then, that the chain of command was poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "We did not have the detailed information about the workings of the headquarters," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not know about and did not ask about the structure of the headquarters, and we did not -- of the staff, of the equipment that was in the headquarters, and we did not have access, for very obvious reasons, to combat orders, orders issued by the various headquarters. But we did have access to and were frequently involved with orders for cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you get to that, you say that generally you believe command and control in the HVO, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone during your tour of duty was poor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can he just use another word but "flimsy"? Can you describe it better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Weak," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He couldn't reach his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "flimsy," by that I mean weak, that it was not a strong chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why that was the case if you know specifically, or why you believe that to be the case if you don't have direct information concerning the internal workings of the HVO in Central Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The indicators that tended for us to believe that this was the case were the poor quality of the officers who were commanding that we came across, and indeed the poor quality of the soldiers. We didn't know a great deal about the communications, but what we knew was that it was of poor quality, but possibly the strongest indicator was that we knew that the small units we came across on the ground were -- their loyalties were quite often different from what we would expect within a military structure. Their loyalties were -- I mentioned this yesterday, but their loyalties were with respect to local politicians and figures. There was a great deal of criminal activity and profiteering conducted by armed uniformed gangs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that poor quality of officers contributed to poor command and control by General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic. Which officers are you referring to, officers in general or which officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My particular knowledge, my expert knowledge, is in relation to the brigade level of command. They were the officers that I dealt with the most. Generally, across the board, the brigade level of command was -- the people who held those positions, those ranks, were of poor quality certainly when compared with a standard British army officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit D418 could be provided to the witness, and folded so that the Travnik/Novi Travnik area is visible on the ELMO, please. It's a JNA map. We used it yesterday. It's the Zenica 3 series map. There were two of them. If we could place that on the ELMO so the circled location is visible, please. Zoom back just a touch, please, if the technical booth could. Very good. Thank you. What I would ask now, Mr. Whatley, is you've told us that you believe the command and control that Colonel Blaskic was able to exercise was poor. Can you think of a particular example that might illustrate this for the Court, and please use the map if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking a moment ago about the brigade level of command, but a much more easily understood example of where the chain of command was not functioning properly was in relation to checkpoints, and I'm now going to, with your permission, go into some detail about an incident that took place at one particular checkpoint. The date of this incident I cannot remember, but I believe it was either March or April '93. If I could ask you to look at the map here. This is the town of Travnik, and the road that comes out of Travnik this way goes down here towards Vitez and the British base, and this road junction here, which was a critical road junction, goes south through Novi Travnik and then down eventually to Gornji Vakuf and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the road junction that is circled with a black circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, this road junction here. From the day we arrived to the day we left and for a long time after, this road junction was the scene of an HVO roadblock, and the size of the roadblock would -- in other words, the number of weapons and people at this roadblock would go up or down depending on the tension and the situation in the local area and in middle Bosnia generally. This was a critical roadblock to the HVO. All our resupply and all our convoys coming up from Croatia went through that roadblock, and all aid agencies and UNHCR agencies coming to middle Bosnia, almost all, came through that junction and that roadblock as well. Quite often we would provide a Warrior escort to aid agencies. This was part of our mandate, and nearly all convoys, and aid agencies and UNHCR convoys were escorted by our soldiers in Warrior fighting vehicles. On one particular occasion, I was not at the checkpoint, I was in my Land Rover somewhere else, and I received a radio message to go to this checkpoint because there was a problem. The details of the problem were not given to me over the radio, but when I arrived at the checkpoint it became obvious what had happened. A British platoon, that is four Warrior vehicles commanded by an officer was escorting a large UNHCR aid convoy. The convoy, which was an UNHCR, in other words, United Nations sponsored convoy with an UNPROFOR escort, had been stopped by the HVO Military Police at this junction. I made an assessment of what the situation was. I spoke to the British commander of the convoy first. I then asked the UNHCR representative to show me some paperwork to confirm, in my mind, that this was the correct convoy, that it was an United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees convoy, and then I went to speak to the HVO commander at the checkpoint, the Military Police in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. How could you tell that the Military Police of the HVO were manning this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew very well in advance who was manning which checkpoint, but they were dressed in HVO uniforms with HVO badges on their arms, HVO cap badges on their caps. They were Military Police which could be told by them wearing white belts and white cross-straps, vertical straps. The checkpoint was very well reinforced with sandbags and RPG, which is a rocket propelled grenade, which would take out -- if it hit the vehicle in the right place would take out a Warrior. I spoke to the military policeman in charge of the checkpoint, and I was with my interpreter, of course, and I said, "Why have you stopped this convoy?"
