He said, "There are Muslims in the convoy, and we don't want the convoy to come down this road." Now, it is true that some of the drivers of some of the trucks were locals. He said that he did not want the convoy to come down this road, and I said to him that whether he wanted it to come down this road or not, this was an U.N. Convoy with a British escort, and the convoy was going to come through this checkpoint and it was going to Zenica, to the UNHCR main warehouse for middle Bosnia. He said, "No way at all." I went outside and I spoke to the platoon commander and I told him, the British platoon commander, and I told him to reposition his Warriors, take them off the road, put them on the ground around, point all the barrels of the main weapons at the checkpoint and be prepared to destroy the checkpoint on my orders. I then went back into the checkpoint and spoke to the checkpoint commander again, the Croat. I said to him, "Have you got a telephone here?" He said, "Yes." So we called -- I had my notebook full of telephone numbers, which I have here, and I called directly to Colonel Blaskic's office, and he knew my voice. I identified myself over the telephone to him, although I couldn't speak Serbo-Croat, and of course, he couldn't speak English. I then gave the telephone receiver to my interpreter, and through her I explained where I was and that this HVO checkpoint had illegally stopped a British and United Nations convoy. He told me that the checkpoint was acting contrary to orders, and that he would tell the checkpoint commander that himself. The interpreter then gave the hand-set of the telephone to the checkpoint commander, and the interpreter then translated the half of the conversation that she could hear. I can't remember the details, but basically the checkpoint commander ended up swearing at Colonel Blaskic and telling him that, I won't use the words, but they weren't polite, and he ended up slamming the phone down on him, and the checkpoint commander was very angry. I could only deduce that the checkpoint commander had been ordered to let the convoy through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In return, he had done what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had apparently sworn at his commander and slammed the phone down on him. I don't know if he refused to let the convoy through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do after the phone call was completed and he hung up on Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I then said to him that if he did not let the convoy through as he had been ordered to, and as he knew he should, that I would ensure that his checkpoint was destroyed and could never interfere with us again. He knew I was serious. He knew me because I had been to that checkpoint many times. I then got into my Land Rover and drove 200 or 300 metres down the road. I then gave an order to the British commander of the Warrior, an order which is well documented in the battalion radio operator's log, that when I give the instruction for the convoy to move, if anyone from the HVO interrupts that convoy, he is to destroy the checkpoint. Luckily that wasn't required and the convoy was not interrupted from that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the phone call between the checkpoint commander and Colonel Blaskic was concluded, did the checkpoint commander allow the convoy to pass at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not straight away. I continued to argue for a minute or two, and then I explained to him that these Warriors outside were going to kill him if he did not let the convoy through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described the level of command and control that Colonel Blaskic had in your view, generally, over the HVO and Central Bosnia as poor, and you've given an example concerning convoys and this very important checkpoint at the Novi Travnik T-junction. Can we perhaps go to another level of detail or specificity, and I would ask you in that regard, can you give the Court your assessment of the degree of command and control that Colonel Blaskic had over HVO forces in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, specifically, with respect to combat activity, not with respect to checkpoints or shining boots or something else, but combat activity. The use of weapons or the failure to use in combat, what was his level of command and control with respect to such activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never knew. We had no access to combat orders. We had no access to knowledge about the intentions of the HVO or the Bosnian army, what they were going to attack. Where we drew most of our conclusions on this matter, from the point of view of written orders and failing to obey orders, was in the realms of cease-fires. We were frequently involved with the cease-fire agreements. Many of these cease-fire agreements were signed by Colonel Blaskic, himself. These were local and regional cease-fires, and because we were BRITBAT, because we were the United Nations and because of our close liaison with the warring factions, this is after April the 16th, we were frequently involved with attempting to monitor the cease-fires, to supervise the cease-fires, to confirm neutrally that both sides had implemented their part of the bargain, their part of the agreement, whether it was forces withdrawing some distance from a given line, or whether it was -- many examples I can't think of at the moment. We were constantly involved in monitoring and supervising cease-fires, which were written orders issued from the respective headquarters on both sides. What we found, generally, was that on both sides, cease-fires were very badly implemented, if at all. Quite often an order to cease-fire at a particular time, and one of our call signs, one of our Warriors would go along to that particular area at the time and there would be no reduction in shooting. Forces were meant to withdraw to certain lines and there would be no withdrawing of forces and no filling in of trenches. There was outright refusal on occasions to respond to any of these orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How then, overall, would you characterise, based on the information that you did have, the level of, the degree of command and control over combat activity or the failure to initiate or engage in combat activity that Colonel Blaskic had in the Central Bosnian region at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The level of command and control would have to be described as poor, when compared with what I would be used to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, with respect to combat type activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already explained about combat activity, but military activity, checkpoint, cease-fires, failing to respond to written and verbal orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The opinions you have given concerning the poor level of command and control within the HVO from the Operative Zone headquarters in Central Bosnia during your tour of service, was this opinion shared by others in the British Battalion at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly shared by Bob Stewart, the commanding officer, and it was certainly shared by the other liaison officers. Generally I didn't discuss such matters with other people in the battalion, so I cannot speak for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could bring Exhibit 29 back around in front of the easel, with the usher's assistance. We're going to play a short videotape in a moment, Mr. President, but I would like to identify what I believe is the location of the events on the videotape before we play the tape. We don't need to actually put it up. Perhaps, I can even come over and hold it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this large map, Exhibit 29, are you able to point out the location of Kasagici on this map? I would direct your attention to the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could step back. First, could you indicate perhaps Busovaca and Kiseljak by way of orientation? Where is Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Busovaca, here, and this is the town of Kiseljak, down here. The village in question, Kasagici, is here, on the north side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Kasagici within the Central Bosnian Operative Zone of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have a short tape from the British Broadcasting Corporation, Mr. President, and I would ask that the lights be dimmed and that it be played at this time. It's approximately three minutes in length. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May we pause the tape? The date, Mr. President, it's a little difficult to see, but it's toward the top, 28 April, 1993. Perhaps if you could rewind the tape for just three or four seconds, and then continue it. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I more or less understand, but I would have preferred to have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we have a French interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I always show indulgence toward the interpreters. I have a general understanding, but I would like to try to get more of the details, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can say, Mr. President, there will be a brief interview with Colonel Robert Stewart, and that would be the most critical portion to be translated, if it could be. Perhaps, if it's difficult, I don't remember how quickly he is speaking, we can play that very short segment more than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hayman, but I'm sure the interpreters will do their best, and then my learned colleagues will help me, too, if I miss one of the nuances in the cassette. Go ahead. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can stop the tape there, please. That's the segment we wish to play, Mr. President. We can turn the lights back on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to thank the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Whatley, the situation described by your commanding officer in Bosnia, Colonel Stewart, of local forces acting wholly independent of a cease-fire order by their headquarters, is that a situation that you learned of repeatedly during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the HVO in Central Bosnia characterised by a comprehensive chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not a military way of describing a chain of command, but the chain of command did not function well, and I think I've given you some examples as to why we believed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic have a firm grip on HVO troops in the Lasva Valley and full control of all local commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understood it, as we believed at the time, command and control was poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the British Battalion aware whether Colonel Blaskic undertook or initiated any investigation of the events in Ahmici in the middle of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're unaware of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether he did or not, it was not something that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree with the statement, the following statement: "The attack on Ahmici could not have occurred without the authority and order of Colonel Blaskic, due to the number of troops involved and the scale of the attack."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree. That statement assumes that all attacks would have to be ordered by Blaskic, and I think that the command and control that existed at the time means it is probably not the case, almost certainly not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the days following the 16th of April, 1993, what were your duties? Were your duties changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the situation in my area of responsibility, an area which I described to you yesterday, became quite intensive, and so, another captain was brought down, another liaison officer was transferred from Tuzla back to Vitez to support me, and I was, and he took on the responsibility for the town of Vitez, and I was tasked to spend all my time in Travnik and Novi Travnik in an attempt to ensure that a Muslim Croat war did not start in either of those two towns. The exact date that this happened, I cannot remember, but it was sometime after the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your service and your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, were you aware whether Colonel Blaskic had access to a helicopter to use to move around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware during my tour that any helicopters flew into Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty did the British Battalion track the movement of HVO artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know we were not in the habit of tracking the movement of any artillery pieces or tanks. We did know the whereabouts of one, you could say permanently stationed large artillery piece, and that was, I could indicate it on the map, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can describe the location, that will be adequate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was within about half a kilometre of our base. It was in a quarry near Mali Mosulj, and we never saw this artillery piece, but we knew it was. There, it was guarded, and I did make one attempt to visit it to confirm what type of piece it was, but we were denied access. Colonel Bob Stewart did not want to antagonise the situation by forcing our way into their military positions, which was not our policy. They told us it was a 203 millimetre gun. That was never confirmed. We knew that one was there, and to the best of my knowledge that one did not move from that location. Throughout the rest of our area of responsibility, if we saw artillery moving or firing, or we saw tanks, then that would be reported. But, no, we did not track them and we did not follow them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it obvious to British Battalion artillery experts that Serb artillery on the Vlasic feature was not in range of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by British army artillery experts in Vitez. We had no members of the Royal Artillery, to the best of my knowledge, to answer that first half of the question. The second half of the question relates to the Serb artillery being in range of Zenica. Throughout my tour, towards the ends of '92 and the beginning of '93, the Serbs, the VRS, did drop artillery shells onto Zenica, and onto many other towns, as well, including Travnik and Zepce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any units or officers of the army of the Republic of Croatia or the HV in the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. We were constantly hearing rumours of the presence of the Croatian army, the army of the Republic of Croatia, or the HV, were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were always hearing these rumours. But I never saw them. No one else that I can remember ever saw them in the Lasva Valley or in Kiseljak. The only occasion I ever saw an HV badge was in -- I visited a bar with an HVO commander on one occasion, and one of his bodyguards had an HVO badge on one arm, and on the other arm had an HV badge which had been held on with a safety pin. That's the only occasion I ever saw an HV badge in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a specific rumour at one point in your tour of duty that there was an HV unit in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was spoken about. We did a little bit of investigating, and the only outsiders we found in Novi Travnik was an outside unit that had come from Mostar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An outside unit of what army, what force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an HVO unit that had come from Mostar that I was aware of in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with the BH army commanders in Vitez and/or Kruscica on the night of the 15th of April, 1993, did they suggest in any way, or did anything they did suggest to you that they were distracted or preoccupied with events in Srebrenica to the east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Srebrenica never became a topic of conversation at all, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer certain exhibits to be admitted into evidence. I believe they are D414, 415, 415A, 416, 417, 417A, 418, 419, 420, 421, and a portion of the tape we played, which I believe will be marked as Defence Exhibit 422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you concluded your examination-in-chief, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If there is no objection to the exhibits and they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then I have concluded my direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I want to compliment you at the same time for having made efforts to be as concise as you can in the questions that you asked. Now, let me turn to the Prosecutor. Will it be Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whatley, you are now going to be asked questions by the Office of the Prosecutor as part of the cross-examination, and following that the Judges will ask you questions which they wish to ask. Mr. Harmon, the floor is yours. Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who was your commanding officer while you were in the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second in command of the Cheshire Regiment was whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first four-and-a-half or five months it was Major Tim Park, and then from, for about three months it was Major Brian Watters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Lieutenant Colonel Martin Thomas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a major at the time, and he commanded a company that moved, but spent quite a lot of time in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those three officers, Colonel Stewart, Lieutenant Colonel Brian Watters and Lieutenant Colonel Martin Thomas are officers who had far more experience than you in the British army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those three officers, correct me if I'm wrong, but those three officers have all had posts at battalion levels and commanded battalion level operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At what stage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any stage in their career, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, subsequently, yes, but at the time in question, Colonel Bob Stewart was the only one of those officers to have had any experience in commanding a battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brian Watters has subsequently taken command of the Cheshire Regiment; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the first battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Martin Thomas has also taken battalion level command in respect of the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you arrived in Bosnia on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1992. You subsequently drove through the town of Prozor, as you described in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you travel through Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the whole of my tour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, probably five or six times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you drove through was approximately the 18th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony on direct examination, was, as I recall, that the situation in Prozor was quite tense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that approximately a week later the HVO attacked the city of Prozor and the Muslims were driven from that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, sir, the Muslims were ethnically cleansed from Prozor; am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to speak a little bit more slowly. You're both speaking the same language, and it is not always easy to distinguish between the question and the answer. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, we both speak the same language, if you would pause briefly after I ask the question to allow the interpreters time to interpret for the Judges and the gallery, everyone would be appreciative. Now, did the ethnic cleansing of Prozor that occurred in October 1992 cause an increase in tensions in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges how and why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem with what happened in Prozor was that it resulted in the collapse of the defence of the town of Jajce. Jajce is, unfortunately, not on this map here. Jajce is well to the west of this map. At about the time we're talking, the town of Jajce was jointly defended by the HVO and the Bosnian army. But the problems in Prozor that we're talking about, which were not unique in Prozor, there were a lot of problems in other towns, as well, at the time, resulted in a loss of confidence in the defence of Jajce, because the HVO and the Bosnian army that were defending Jajce together knew their families back in the other towns like Prozor were involved in a war against the families of the soldiers they were jointly defending Jajce with. Consequently, there was a loss of morale and a loss of confidence in Jajce, and the Serbs took Jajce very quickly. The result was a huge convoy, an almost endless convoy, and it was one of the saddest things, of refugees leaving the town with whatever they could get their hands on and heading east towards the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, let me focus exclusively on the effect of the ethnic cleansing of Mostar on the Muslim community in Central Bosnia. Did the ethnic cleansing of Prozor cause alarm in Travnik, in Novi Travnik, in Vitez, in Busovaca, in Kiseljak and in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about Prozor? I thought you said Mostar. You're talking about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You said Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come to Mostar in a few minutes. Let's stay with Prozor for a minute. Tell us, please, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the effect on the Muslim community in the municipalities which I just identified, the effect of the ethnic cleansing of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The effects of the ethnic cleansing in Prozor was the collapse of Jajce. The effect of the collapse of Jajce, if I may continue, was that the towns of Travnik and Vitez and Novi Travnik and other towns in Central Bosnia became even more full of refugees. The ethnic balances were further displaced. That was the most obvious affect to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you then a less obvious effect to you, sir. Did the Muslims in the communities which I've identified become fearful and distrustful of the HVO as a result of the HVO ethnically cleansing Muslims from Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was probably more difficult to maintain the alliance, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Prozor, you had been through there a number of times --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say I'm not trying to be evasive here, but what the Prosecutor is asking me is that was not how we saw it at the time. I'm trying to be as honest as I can here. What we saw at the time was a huge refugee problem, and a general decrease in the confidence between the two sides. We did not see alarm and panic because the overwhelming day-to-day functions of the HVO and the Bosnian army, at this time, were in the fight against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your principle job, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, was to mingle, if you will, the communities where you were a liaison officer. You mingled with civilians, with representatives of the Bosnians, Muslims, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Serbs. My question very directly to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's two questions, Mr. President. He's just stated a proposition and now he's asking a question. Let the witness answer whether the first statement is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please, if I could ask the question. If the witness is confused in some way, it's up to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind everybody of the difficulty the interpreters have when they have to work under those circumstances. For me it's difficult as well. I'm not speaking for my colleagues but it's very difficult for me as well. I haven't heard the end of the question when the answer begins. Mr. Hayman is correct. Make your comment, but try to get to your first question directly and then ask your second one, and then in ten minutes we'll take our break. I would like to say that for the interpreters' sake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I accurately state what your responsibilities were in part, to mingle with, and to understand, and to have your ear to the ground in respect of the military and civil leaders of the various ethnic groups in the area where you were a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is one way of describing my responsibilities. I didn't use the word "mingle," but yes, I had to deal primarily with the military commanders, and, secondly, the civilian leaders in my areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslim civilians, the civilian leaders, and the military leaders more distrustful of the HVO as a result of the burning of houses in Prozor, as a result of the driving out of the Muslim civilian population, as a result of the ethnic cleansing that occurred in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's quite an accurate way of describing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn, if I can, very briefly to your responsibilities here as a liaison officer. Initially, when you arrived in Central Bosnia, you told us that your area of responsibility was from Maglaj to Zenica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you have those particular responsibilities in that area of operation? From what date to what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what date I was first sent up there or should I say when it was first decided I would have that responsibility. It would have been -- that decision was probably made in the first week of November 1992, and then I eventually relinquished or handed over that area in the first week of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In between the 1st of November of 1992 and the first week of March of 1993, you took some leave time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, I did, sorry. I took two weeks' leave in January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also take a week's leave in late February or early March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you -- now, in respect of the other areas where other liaison officers operated, Captain Martin Foregrave was responsible during that time frame for Travnik, Novi Travnik and Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with me as his shadow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what you mean by "shadow"? I didn't understand that term yesterday in your direct-examination. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant that if for any reason he could not be there, for example, two weeks' leave in December, then I would take responsibility. At any other time, if for some reason, and I can explain some of the reasons, but if for some reason I didn't go to my area, I would probably spend all day with him in his area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, between the first of November, first week in November of 1992 and first week in March 1993, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, how much time did you spend in his area of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the two weeks that he was away on leave -- I spent most of the week before he went on leave with him refreshing my knowledge, and I probably spent one or two days a week every week before that, something of that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in charge also of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to Captain Foregrave, Captain Mark Cooper was involved with Tuzla as the liaison officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Captain Mark Cooper the liaison officer in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the two liaison officers in Tuzla, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other was Captain Bob Ryan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vares, was Captain John Ellis the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He became the liaison officer very late in the tour. I don't know when. I think probably January or February. Maybe before, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who preceded him, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think there was a liaison officer before him down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, was Captain Mike Hughes the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've described primarily your liaison responsibilities in respect of the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, but to give a fuller and more robust picture, you also had liaison responsibilities with the Bosnian Serbs, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your responsibilities with the Bosnian Serbs included both the area where you were initially assigned, that is Maglaj and Zenica, and then where you were subsequently assigned, which was the Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Vitez and Travnik municipalities; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you're not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please correct me then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in my first area I did not deal with the Serbs in the northern area at all. However, while I was in the northern area, responsible still for the northern area, I dealt with the Serbs west of Travnik. I never had any dealings with the Serbs in the northern area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you remained, as I believe you testified, you remained as the liaison officer in the Vitez, Travnik, Busovaca and Zenica area until sometime after April the 16th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, it was, I believe, Bob Ryan who became the liaison officer in the Vitez municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I don't know exactly when that happened, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you check your notebook to see when that happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not in my notebook. I've attempted to decipher this but it doesn't actually say that. This is only a record of the meetings I held. It's not a diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have an approximate recollection of when that was, sometime after April 16th, but you don't have a precise recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your working as a liaison officer, you testified yesterday that it was very, very important to develop a very close relationship with the commanders and the civil leaders of all of the ethnic groups with whom you were performing liaison functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, and I should emphasise it was particularly important to develop a relationship with the military commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Well, first of all, I would be very interested in your identifying for us, please, the military leaders and political leaders with whom you developed a close relationship who were on the Bosnian Serb side. Could you please tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not develop relationships with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember any of the commanders in your area of operation who were Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and if you want me to explain this, I will. I'm surprised that you're asking this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please, you can answer it anyway you'd like, but my question is: Can you identify any of the Bosnian Serb political leaders or military leaders with whom you had liaison relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I can remember a couple of names. The name Grujicic comes to mind, and Poletan and a few other names. The reason for this, if I can explain, Mr. President? We lived in Vitez, and Vitez was part of Muslim Croat territory, which only -- at my time, only was 30 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The other 70 per cent was in the hands of the Serbs. Between us and the Serbs was a major front-line, a very well-defended, well-established front-line. We, the British, had no basis in the Republika Srpska, in the Serb Bosnia. When we went across there it was arranged from Travnik. It was arranged by me over the radio from the radio operations room in Travnik of the Bosnian army through Baba Salko, a very brave man, and he would cross the front-lines with us. We would stay there for two or three hours for meetings or picking up prisoners of war, or shall I say refugees, and escorting them back, or we'd had long meetings discussing local cease-fires in that area to allow us to do that type thing. We would then travel back to our base in Vitez. I did this 17 times. I was the first British officer to cross the Serb front-line, but no, I did not develop the type of relationships which counsel is talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any opportunity at all to meet the paramount military and political leaders from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the paramount military of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the paramount military leader at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no occasion to meet them in your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I see it's time we should have a break, and I'm prepared to stop at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. We will resume the hearing now. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, I have been informed that we are going too fast in our questions and answers, so I am going to make a considerable effort to slow my pace, and if you would also hesitate after I ask you a question, it would slow your pace, and everyone in the courtroom who assists would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we left when discussing the leaders with whom you had had contact on the Serb side, and now I'd like to focus your attention, during the time period when you were a liaison officer, from the first week of March until the end of your tour as a liaison officer. Could you please identify for the Court and for me the military and the political leaders on the Bosnian Muslim side with whom you had liaison relations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I may have to refer to a bit of paper here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could that, please, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, in each of the communities. If you could break it down into Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik and Zenica. It would be sufficient, rather than writing them down, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, if you could just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we could start with Zenica then. My main point of contact in Zenica was the headquarters of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian army, and I had occasion there to occasionally pass messages and meet the corps commander whose name was Enver Hadzihasanovic. More usually I would probably meet one of his deputies, Dzemal Merdan, who -- and also Esad Dzenanovic. They were the principle deputies that I spoke to there. Up until the 15th of April, 1993, I had no connection with the HVO in Zenica. If we could then go now to Travnik. My main point of contact on the Bosnian government side in Travnik was Baba Salko, but I also had constant contact with Commander Kulenovic and Colonel Alagic. These are military commanders. I'm going through the military people at the moment. On the HVO side, the Croat side of Travnik, my main contact was Filipovic, and then he was replaced by Commander Leotar. In Novi Travnik, on the -- the microphone has gone dead here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're fine. It's still on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik -- I'm getting the French here. Have I pressed a button? It's come back now. No, it's gone again. It's coming and going. I've got French on -- okay. Sorry. I hit the wrong one. In Novi Travnik the HVO commander for the period you asked me, who I had constant dealings with was Zeljko Sabljic, and the Bosnian army military commanders that I dealt with were Mevludin Zarajpe (phoen) and Berberovic Mevludin. The pronunciation is very difficult for me. In Busovaca, I didn't go often to Busovaca but when I did go there I occasionally met the -- the name is not in my book here. It will come to me in a moment, the HVO commander there. Very occasionally I went to Kacuni, which was in the Busovaca opstina but it was the Bosnian army headquarters and I occasionally met the commander down there. I'm afraid I don't remember their names. There is a list of other people I did meet in Busovaca here, but these were not the principle people. I very seldom went there. In Vitez, still continuing on the military side, the principle military commander I met in Vitez with was Mario Cerkez, and the Bosnian army commanders I met in Vitez -- in the town of Vitez was Sefkija Dzidic, but also I would meet the commanders down at Kruscica and Preocica, which were also battalion commanders outside of the town, but I'm afraid I don't remember their names and I don't really know if they're in this book. Their meetings were towards the end -- after the 16th of April, when things became a little bit more chaotic, and so their names do not appear in this book because this book was written before then. With regards to the civilian leaders that I would meet, in Vitez I met, on occasions, Santic and Skopljak, one of which, and I can never remember which one. One was the mayor and one was the President of the HDZ on the Croat side. I did not meet any civilian leaders routinely on the Muslim side in Vitez, on the Bosnian government side. In Zenica I very seldom met civilians. I met the President of the rugby club and various people but not routinely. In Busovaca I don't believe I met any civilians on a routine basis. In Novi Travnik probably not. In Travnik I occasionally met the mayor, and some HDZ representatives occasionally who were hanging around the HVO headquarters, but I'm afraid I can't remember the names of them either. All these names are in one of these books somewhere, but it is a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, based on your recollections, in respect of the civil leaders of both the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, it seems or sounds to me like you had minimum or virtually no contact with them as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did meet civilians frequently, but what I'm trying to say is I don't remember their names and it was -- I would not always meet the same one. It was quite often I would just bump into civilians, because my main efforts, you may understand, was towards the military commanders, but that's not to say the civilians leaders didn't know who I was. I remember attending a couple of very large meetings in Travnik chaired by the mayor, one of which had two or three hundred people in a hall, and I was rather surprised that, as I entered the hall, I was cheered by the assembled people. Apparently, they knew who I was even if I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a meeting with the Bosnian Croat civil leaders did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That one in Travnik would have been the Muslims, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muslims. All right. Now, let me ask you, you didn't mention Colonel Blaskic. Did you liaise with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on a lesser extent. I think I explained that earlier. My primary role was to maintain a constant relationship with the brigade levels, but I did frequently attend his hotel, his office, his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with Colonel Blaskic while you were a liaison officer in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember how many times I met him. It's very difficult to remember. The number of times I went to his headquarters with a view to either meeting him or passing a message to him was probably 20. The numbers of times I actually met him, I can only actually, specifically remember two times that I actually sat and talked to him, and I would normally meet him as I was acting as aid to Colonel Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when were those two times that you sat and talked to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was in October '92 and one was in May '93 that I can specifically remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting in October of 1992 when you were introduced as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your meeting with him in May of 1993 when you were leaving the theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Other than those two occasions, the only other occasions you met with Colonel Blaskic as a liaison officer was as an aid or an assistant with Colonel Stewart, your commanding officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or I would -- primarily, but I -- there were other occasions. I'm sure I met him, but I say I can't specifically remember any occasions. But there were the other occasions where I would go to Hotel Vitez with the view of passing a message to him, or asking him for a meeting, or asking him for a document, this type of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the two occasions that you do recall, meeting Colonel Blaskic, October, 1992 and May of 1993, those were meetings where matters of substance were not discussed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you a little bit about the Hotel Vitez, because you say you went there what, approximately 20 times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be rather more. It is a long time ago to remember but it may be more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're familiar with the Hotel Vitez, suffice it to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where would you normally meet the liaison officers that you dealt with in the Hotel Vitez? First of all, did you meet with liaison officers normally in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the local military commands, both Bosnian army and HVO, didn't institute a system of liaison officers until the regiment that came after my regiment. During my time, we dealt with commanders, and if they weren't available then their staff officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the Hotel Vitez? When you walked in, first of all, did you have to pass a checkpoint or a guard to gain access into the interior of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not normally, no, I didn't. Although there was a lot of security on the hotel, I would not normally be expected to go through any checks because the staff there knew me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. But if they didn't know you, would you normally be stopped by a security person or a security post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end, when everyone was getting very twitchy in April or May, normally I would not walk straight in past the security, round and round again into Colonel Blaskic's office. Normally we would stop en route and be intercepted by a staff officer, and he would then want to know the nature of the visit, and would either take me in to deal with Colonel Blaskic myself, personally, to hand over a document, pass a message or whatever, arrange a meeting, or he would ask if he could handle it himself because Colonel Blaskic was too busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things you mentioned yesterday when you were discussing your role as a liaison officer was that your job required you not to make probing inquiries into matters that may be sensitive to any of the parties. Does that fairly characterise your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but if I could explain, that that was how we, as liaison officers, sat down. You mentioned Martin Foregrave earlier on. He and I worked closely for the whole of the time we were there, and we discussed our best strategy and that was it. This wasn't ordained from on high, this was the way we decided to operate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But your personal modus operandi was not to make inquiries into sensitive matters unless it was a matter of conflict and matter that had been tabled, and it was a matter of dispute by the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I would refrain from asking what I considered to be sensitive questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you were aware of what occurred in Ahmici, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At some point, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you attend the meeting with Colonel Stewart where Colonel Stewart confronted Colonel Blaskic about what occurred in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you. Did you attend such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do have a recollection of that, but it may help if I refer to my notebook briefly. I may find the meeting in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall such a meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't mean to be evasive, but I think probably, yes, that meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, normally it was for Colonel Stewart to raise matters that were sensitive with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it in your meetings with either Colonel Blaskic or with other HVO officers with whom you had contact, generally, the subordinates of Colonel Blaskic, you didn't raise the issue of Ahmici with them, did you, for fear that that might endanger your relationship with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Colonel Blaskic's level of command I certainly would not have asked questions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you raise questions of that nature with Colonel Blaskic's subordinates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're telling this Court, at no time did you, as a British liaison officer, make any inquiry into the responsibilities and the events at Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct. I'll explain it, because I don't want the Court to be misled on this issue. The Cheshire Regiment, my regiment, we did not become aware of the events in Ahmici until some days after the event. Prior to us becoming aware of the horrific events in Ahmici, I, or at about the same time, another liaison officer came and took over the area of Vitez and Ahmici from me, and he went ahead and supervised the burial of the 96 bodies. He was, from that point on, the primary liaison officer for Vitez, as I concentrated on the west of Travnik and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your dealings with your military counterparts in the HVO in Travnik and Novi Travnik, I take it you did not inquire into the well-known events at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the information we received was from the Bosnian army representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the information you received, as well, about what occurred in Ahmici was from your own forces at BRITBAT; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you were fully aware of the extent of the destruction and the killing at Ahmici; were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a point in time when we did become fully aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That time was in April of 1993; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was approximately April 22nd or April 23rd of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, in terms of other inquiries that you had the ability to make, such as who was responsible for the truck bomb explosion that occurred in Stari Vitez, did you raise issues of responsibility for that crime with any HVO representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider what occurred at Stari Vitez with the truck bomb to be a war crime, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a crime of the most horrific order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a war crime which, if you were a commander of an operation, you would conduct an investigation; would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you conduct an investigation if that war crime occurred on your watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean if a subordinate of mine planted a truck bomb in a town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously the Muslims didn't plant the truck bomb; did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck bomb was almost certainly planted by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were a Croat commander, if you were Colonel Blaskic, would you initiate an inquiry into responsibilities relating to that truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, Mr. President. It seems we're going to go for another three weeks on cross-examination if this is the scope of cross-examination of this witness, and I would ask the Court to give some guidance. How long is cross-examination going to be allowed? I think the direct was three hours or three hours and twenty minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this line of inquiry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The direct examination lasted how long? I'm not sure. Was it about three hours, Mr. Hayman? Yes, I think we have to try to maintain a certain balance. I would not like the previous example of testimony to reappear. I did compliment the Defence for its conciseness. It is true, Mr. Harmon, that perhaps you have asked questions, what would you have done under this or that circumstance. I think that the former officer is here to answer your questions in respect of what he was able to observe while he was exercising his functions. Therefore, perhaps you shouldn't ask the same question several times. Please continue. In fact, we're going to start timing the cross-examination, but we haven't got to that point, yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will conclude within the time frame allotted to me. But this witness has made numerous comparisons between the British army and the HVO, and my question to him, I believe, is relevant, because it asks this witness as a professional military, former professional military officer what he would have done under similar circumstances, which I believe would be relevant to this Court's determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is your evaluation. Let me remind you of what the registrar just told me. There was three hours and 45 minutes in the direct examination, three hours and 45 minutes, the registrar's just told me that. Thank you Mr. Dubuisson. Continue Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, please, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I had been a British military commander in a war and one of my subordinates, or a unit operating under my command and in my area of responsibility committed such a horrific war crime, yes, using the British military justice system and all legal powers available to me, and the duty as a military commander, yes, I would have conducted an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you about some additional testimony that you gave yesterday, and that dealt with the issue of a large troop movement that occurred on the 8th of April in Travnik. Do you remember testifying to that on that occasion you were informed by, I believe it was Colonel Filipovic, that there was a movement of approximately 500 Bosnian army soldiers on the 8th of April, and that you considered that to be a large troop movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I do remember saying that Colonel Filipovic considered it to be a large troop movement, and that is why it was brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider that to be a large troop movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think at the time and in the location it probably was, otherwise Colonel Filipovic would not have brought it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That fact having been brought to your attention, did you go and talk to Colonel Alagic and inquire of Colonel Alagic about that particular large troop movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mind if I just consult my notebook?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening I had, I think I had two further meetings in Travnik, one was at the police station with the civilian police commander, to follow-up the point about police not doing enough. Then I went to the Bosnian army headquarters in Travnik where I was told that two members of 312 Brigade, Bosnian army brigade, had been killed and that the Bosnian army commander, I don't know whether it was Alagic or Cuskic (phoen) on this occasion, asked that I should send the Warriors back into town. That is all my notebook says. I do not know whether I discussed that issue with the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you consider that information that you had received to be vital information at the time you received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I passed all information that I received. I passed to the MILINFO cell. If I, at the time, considered it to be vital I would have gone and found Bob Stewart and told him, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, of having either radioed that information to BRITBAT, having told Colonel Stewart, or told the MILINFO cell about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection, but I almost certainly total the MILINFO cell, because I told them everything in my notebook and an awful lot more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an exhibit--

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have this distributed, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, before this document arrives and is distributed to everybody in the courtroom: Did you have occasion, after you gave information to the military information cell, to check the military information summaries to see if they had properly recorded and reported the information which you provided to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for that was, at the end of each day the last thing I would do each day would be go to the MILINFO cell and be debriefed, a process which may take as much as an hour. Everything I said would be written down, and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be 539.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to receiving information about the 500 Muslim soldiers who had arrived in Travnik, you told us that Colonel Filipovic was going to be moving the HVO headquarters from Travnik to Dolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have the exhibit, 539, in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that appear to be a Cheshire military information summary dated the 8th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention, please, to the last page of that document, page 4, and it says at the top of that "6" and then it says "Travnik." Will you kindly read that to yourself? When you are finished let me know. Actually, I will read it, because we don't have a French translation. It reads as follows: "An LO team visited Travnik this evening and spoke to a BiH officer who claimed that tensions had risen between Croats and Muslims in the town today. The BiH officer claimed that there had been sporadic gunfire for the last 40 minutes at 2000 hours. The LO reported that he had heard two small arms rounds followed by a sustained burst of fire. The BiH officer claimed that Mate Boban had visited Travnik today and subsequently complained about the lack of Croat flags. The BiH officer claimed that a Muslim fired on some HVO soldiers erecting a Croat flag, and from there the situation had deteriorated. At 2100 hours the LO reported that there were groups of armed soldiers moving around the town and tensions appeared to be high. At 2105 hours two RECCE C/S deployed to Travnik and remained there until 2230 hours. At 2230 hours, the LO, meaning liaison officer, reported the situation calmed down somewhat and the RECCE CS were recalled." Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the military information summary that I have just read to you makes no reference at all to the arrival of 500 Muslim soldiers in the town of Travnik; does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor does it make any mention of the movement of the HVO headquarters from Travnik to Dolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what did you believe to be the purpose of the arrival of those 500 soldiers in Travnik on April the 8th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware, sir, that the Bosnian army was engaged in conflicts in Visoko with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This bus, or buses with, according to Colonel Filipovic, 500 Muslim soldiers, arrived from Visoko; did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not those 500 soldiers that arrived in Travnik were soldiers who were returning from the front-lines at Visoko on a rotation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no idea about this. I read what my notebook said, which was a result of a conversation I had with a concerned HVO commander in Travnik, an HVO commander for whom I have the greatest respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the information was unconfirmed, as far as other parties verifying that information; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the liaison officer. No one verified what I said. There was no verification procedure. We did not go into barracks and count soldiers. I reported what the commanders told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately a week later, you personally attended a military parade of the ABiH at barracks in Travnik; did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier, and indeed you showed us a photograph of you in attendance at that parade where over 1000 ABiH soldiers were on parade celebrating the first anniversary of the founding of the Armija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to your testimony in respect of training. You were asked the question yesterday, as follows: "Did you, during your six month or so tour, ever see the HVO troops engaged in training?" Your answer was: "No." The next question that was asked to you was: "On any occasions?" Your answer was, "No, I didn't and in the time I was in, in the time I was in Bosnia, I never heard anyone else talk about the training of either the HVO or the Bosnian army." Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, did the HVO have an operations and training officer at the Hotel Vitez at one of Colonel Blaskic's staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Slavko Marin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Slavko Marin by some coincidence at the airport in Amsterdam about six days ago as he was coming to be, or coming to be a witness here. I didn't recognise him. I don't think he recognised me, I don't know, but that's the gentleman of whom you're referring to, and I subsequently found out he had been a staff officer under Colonel Blaskic's headquarters. I did not recognise his face. I may have known him, and I may have known what he did, but he is not in any of my books, and I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Slavko Marin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Saturday?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time since.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask any HVO liaison officers with whom you had contact in your tour of duty in Bosnia whether the HVO was engaged in training activities for its troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I must reiterate, the HVO did not have liaison officers when I was dealing with them. I dealt with commanders, that's the first part of the question. Secondly, I didn't ask them questions of that nature. I did not ask them, didn't ask anyone questions that may make me look like a spy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question: In your tour of Central Bosnia, do you know where the local HVO military bases were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a few of them, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had, to the best of my knowledge, I believe, a large base in Busovaca. They had many bases in and around Vitez that I would drive past and see large numbers of soldiers congregated in. In Travnik I knew they had a bit of a base in the Hotel Orient, and there were lots of small locations, houses and shops, ex-shops and ex-houses where you could see a large number of HVO soldiers on occasions. But if you ask me about their barracks, no, I'm not aware of where the barracks were, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 484 shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, if it's all right, like to clarify something about this MILINFOSUM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the reason why nothing is in my notebook, appears in the MILINFOSUM on this day, and it is quite unusual for my notebook not to appear in the MILINFOSUM. I think the reason for it was I don't think I left Travnik until about 11.00 or midnight in the evening. Because from reading this, and from reading my notebook, I think, I stayed in Travnik until the last possible minute, until very late at night, because I wanted to keep a personal eye on what was happening there. I was probably going from headquarters to headquarters just checking that the commanders felt they were in control. Before I suggested that the British armoured vehicles be removed from Travnik, I would have got, well, not permission, but I would have asked the advice of the Bosnian army commander and the HVO commander. I would have gone to them, as, indeed, I'm sure I did, according to this, and said to them, is the situation calm enough now for the British to go home and have dinner, and they would have both at some point have said yes, and the armoured vehicles would have left and I would have left. I think by the time I would have got back to the British base it would have probably been too late, or whatever, I don't know, but I think that's probably why nothing appeared in this MILINFOSUM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor did you radio this information. Had you radioed this information in, then it would have appeared in the MILINFOSUM; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, from looking at this, that probably I did radio some in, because it says here "At 2100 the LO reported there were groups of armed soldiers moving around the town and tensions appeared to be high." At that time I was either in meetings or between meetings, I think. It's slightly confusing to see in my notebook. Probably I left one meeting, got in my Land Rover and radioed to Vitez that bit of information and gone through to another meeting. It would be during that meeting that I would have probably asked, in fact obviously here, because at 2100 hours I radioed that message in, and at 2105 hours the vehicles, the armoured vehicles were sent to Travnik, so, obviously as a result of my radio message. What I considered to be vital information was passed over the radio, and the battalion, as usual, responded accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have passed, then, that information on the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I would like to see the MILINFOSUM, but it's quite possible by the next morning events had overtaken this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, could I also have at the same time Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/104 through 108? In the meantime I will ask Mr. Dundas-Whatley about the exhibit in front of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the Prosecutor's Exhibit 484? This, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is a training plan and programme for recruits of the HZ-HB armed forces, and it was issued in Mostar on the 1st of September, 1992 by Brigadier General Milvoj Petkovic. Do you know who Milvoj Petkovic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was the commander of the HVO in the whole of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can take a look at this, please. Browse through it for a moment. Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley have you had a chance, briefly at least, to look at that particular training programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a training programme. If you turn to page 3 of the document, it is referring to paragraph 1.2. This is a training programme that lasts 22 days. If you turn the page, to page 4, under paragraph 1.3, you can see the curriculum is summarised in that particular page. Now, this is a training programme that was for recruits of the HZ-HB. I would next like to direct your attention to the following exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/104 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. Dundas-Whatley? It hasn't been given to you yet. Number 104, which you have before you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 23rd of July, 1992, and it is an order which orders a number of soldiers to be trained in the use of a Strella 2-M rocket. Those soldiers were to assemble in front of the Hotel Vitez at 8.00 in the morning on the 25th of July, 1992. If you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 105, this also is an order of Colonel Blaskic, it is dated the 24th of July, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine says the 25th. Right, it's the next one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be. Perhaps the usher can make sure they are given to Mr. Dundas-Whatley in the proper order. I'm talking about Prosecutor's Exhibit 105.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I do apologise, it is dated the 24th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order by Colonel Blaskic to create and train reconnaissance units, and those units were to be trained in Grude, and they were -- obviously the order speaks for itself. If we turn now to Prosecutor's Exhibit 106, this is a document that is three pages long. You should have it in front of you, and it is, if you turn to paragraph 3 of that particular document, an order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 20th of September, 1992. You will see that paragraph 3 relates to the training of new recruits who have not served in the Yugoslav army. It is to be basic and specific, and the person who is responsible for that task is the operations and training body of the central headquarters, and the deadline for that training was the 15th to the 30th of September, 1992. Now, let me turn, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to the next Prosecutor's exhibit, which is 456/107.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have 106.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 456/107, it is a document that looks like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, a document that looks like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order also issued by Colonel Blaskic dated the 19th of November, 1992. Take a look at that for a minute, if you will, and you will see that it is essentially a training regimen. It describes a training schedule that should apply to all barracks in the territory of Central Bosnia and all barracks commanders shall adhere to this particular schedule. You will see, then, quite a schedule. The last document I would like to show you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is a document that is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/108. It is an order dated the 12th of March --
