utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're just looking for this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a one-page document, and it is ordered by Colonel Blaskic that additional training be required for crews of light portable S2MAAD launching systems, and in paragraph number 3, one day refresher courses shall be organised once a month. Now, the sum of these orders, which are merely representational, indicate that from the 23rd of July, 1992, through the 12th of March, 1993, the HVO was engaged in the training of its soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Mr. Harmon is trying to testify. These are orders for training. They don't indicate whether there was training or not. The witness testified orders frequently weren't followed. In any event, he said he didn't see any training, so I think the purpose of this line of inquiry is very hard to discern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Each of you will use the witness as he likes and according to his objectives whether the Defence or the Prosecution strategy. For the time being I think the Prosecution is simply trying to ascertain from the witness whether he was aware of the training. That's not excessive. Of course, don't spend three hours doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, it would not be unusual, would it, sir, that the HVO would not take you to its training facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be unusual for the HVO, or would it be normal for the HVO to take third parties to its training facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be very unusual. These documents are marked secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, it doesn't surprise you, does it, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that the HVO was engaged in the training of its recruits; does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Assumes a fact not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have shown a film. I don't want to delay, taking the time to reshow the film of the HVO engaged in training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where, Your Honour, was that film shot? It was not shot in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. The Counsel's question assumes a fact not in evidence, and he shouldn't be allowed to ask the witness "would it surprise you that," making an assertion of fact when it's a fact not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, as regards to the form of the questions, I think both you and Mr. Harmon are very subtle specialists to know how to ask a question in the direct and cross-examinations. As regards the training, it is undeniable that the liaison officer, through his duties, had access to certain kinds of information that would be useful for our discussions here, which you did bring up in the direct examination. That is the question of training. I once again would like to ask Mr. Harmon not to dwell too long on that question. I think that the question was asked and that the liaison officer answered the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, does it surprise you to see these orders and this training programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not surprised to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to a different subject, then, sir. You were asked a question yesterday as follows: "Did the HVO headquarters in the Central Bosnia Operational Zone have access to secure fax or other secure communications?" Your answer was, "Not that I'm aware of." Do you remember that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the Hotel Vitez, did you have unlimited access to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever permitted into the HVO communications centre in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I did go into the HVO communications centre, which actually was not in Hotel Vitez. It was in the post office in the centre of the town. That was my understanding, anyway. But only on one occasion that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about April, 1993. It was during the very heavy period of conflict in April 1993, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what kind of communications you saw, what kind of communications equipment you saw in that particular location at that particular day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular location and that particular day, I saw a number, probably half a dozen of soldiers in uniform sitting at desks which were manned with -- there were maps on the wall, and they were manning telephones, and there may have been radios, hand-held radios, there, as well. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go into any communications centre of the HVO when you were in Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik or Zenica? I'm talking about communications centres of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever talk to any HVO officers about their communications capabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be useful if I told you what I spoke to the Bosnian army about their communications abilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stay for a moment -- you talked to the HVO about their communications capabilities. Did you ever talk to them about their communications capabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the HVO representatives with whom you were dealing, the officers that you have identified, whether or not they had encryption capabilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who the head of intelligence was for the HVO headquarters at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that he testified in this court that the HVO had encryption capability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the internal workings of the command structure of the HVO were not a major concern of mine. How they conducted their military campaign was not my overriding business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not your testimony, is it, that the HVO did not have secure communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My testimony, and I'm sure it's written down somewhere, I said yesterday that I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in part, you said yesterday that it would be very important to have, essentially -- or be very dangerous -- let me rephrase it. It would be very dangerous to have combat orders sent that were not encrypted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason being if they were intercepted, then it would be almost fatal or suicidal to the attacking forces to -- it would be intercepted; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you, if I could, Prosecutor's exhibit -- I'm sorry, Defence Exhibit 300, and Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/46. Mr. Dubuisson, I will actually make it easier for you. It will be 456/45 and 456/46. Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, I would just like to ask your opinion on something, and perhaps you would be so kind as to review these orders with me first. I would like to refer you to 456/45, which is an order for combat operations issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 17th of April, 1993. It's in English. It is a two-page document, and the time of the issue is 2345 hours. Now, let me just direct your attention to paragraph 2.2 of that particular combat order, and in that it gives direction. It says, "Use all available artillery, carry out fire preparations for the attack from the VU, capture Gornji Zenica and Svinjarevo through systematic targeting (6082 and 120 millimetre MB), afterwards regroup forces and carry out artillery preparations for launching an attack on" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please read more slowly. The interpreters don't have the documents in front of them. The register has given me the version in French. For once I'm the one at an advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the last sentence. "Afterwards, regroup forces and carry out artillery preparations for launching an attack on and the capture of Bilalovac." If you turn to paragraph 10 on the second page it says, "Begin the operation on the 18th of April, 1993 at 0530 hours." So, at the time when this order was issued and the time when it was to be executed is approximately 5 hours and 45 minutes difference. My question to you is: This order was issued from Vitez, and it was issued to the Ban Jelicic Brigade, the command in Kiseljak, and as you know, there was an area of occupied territory by the Muslims between Kacuni and Bilalovac, and this order had to pass through or over that territory in order to be received in Kiseljak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, using your judgement and looking at this document and looking at the time frame that is required from the time the order is issued to the time when it needs to be executed, would it be prudent to send this particular document with either unencrypted or insecure communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe, or can you deduce from just the four corners of this document that this document would have been sent by secure communications if you're able to give us your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Objection to the form, Mr. President. It calls for speculation. That's a ludicrous question if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What I was interested in -- I'm going to put the microphone on. One should not use that kind of language to talk about the questions that your colleagues ask. We have only five minutes left. Try to remain calm. With all the respect I owe you, I don't find the question ridiculous, and I would be very interested in hearing the answer. Continue, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question or do you want me to repeat it, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think I understand. The issue here, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With your permission, our client is actively participating in our work, and he says the following: That probably, by omission, the transcript says that the artillery attack was supposed to be carried out against Gornji Zenica, at the very beginning of this text, so please let's have this corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That clearly is an error, and the document speaks for itself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Are we still talking about using artillery against the area of Kiseljak or some other area now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about this particular order, and my question to you is: Using the four corners of this document, considering that it is an order for combat, it was an order issued on the 17th of April at 2345 hours, with an operation to begin at 5.30 the following day. This is an order that had to pass through or over hostile territory. Can you deduce that this is a document -- are you able to give us an opinion as to whether this document was sent by secure means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So, if it went over enemy territory, so to speak, by radio or any other means, was it sent securely or not? If it could not be taken by hand and it was transmitted over the airwaves, which I think is what you're suggesting, then it would be very stupid not to send it in some coded fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you, because we only have a minute or two remaining. Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/46, which is another combat order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 18th of April, 1993, and let me refer you to paragraph 2 that discusses the assignment of the addressee who was the commander of the Fojnica HVO battalion. In other words, this was going to a different part of Colonel Blaskic's command. Paragraph 2, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, discusses combat operations on the village of Dusina, or discussing a breakthrough in the direction of the Busovaca stables and a linkup with the forces defending Sebisic (phoen), and it discusses preventing the enemy from bringing fresh forces for combat operations to the Lasva Valley, engage some forces to control the area and reduce no-man's land. Again, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the same question I asked you before. This is a combat order that went to a different part of the command of Colonel Blaskic. Again, it went from the Hotel Vitez. It had to go through or over enemy territory, which was the territory that was between Kiseljak municipality and the Vitez Busovaca municipality. I ask you the same question; in your opinion, would this be the order that would have been sent by secure communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information contained in this order would be very dangerous if it fell into the enemy hands, and if it had to be transmitted using the radio, and if it was not sent in code, that would be very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I have no additional questions this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards the amount of time, the Defence used 3 hours and 25 minutes and you used 1 hour and 25 minutes. Therefore, tomorrow, if we begin at 9.45, and taking into account a 20-minute break, you should finish by 5 minutes after 12.00. Of course, we can have a certain degree of flexibility, and that should allow you to focus all of your questions on the objectives which you consider to be essential, and not to subject yourself to the angry comments of Mr. Hayman about the quality of your questions. Having said this, I can give you back the figures and say we will now suspend the hearing and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.02 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of October, 1998, at 9.45 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
